It’s Sunday once more, and you know what that means — it’s time for our weekly social media roundup! This weekend has been yet another veritable whirlwind in the Bronx, as the team celebrated a postseason appearance, bid farewell to a fan favorite, closed an era of minor league baseball, and watched as their Captain hit the shelf once more. With so much in store, let’s get started!
Another Celebration in Minnesota
It was deja vu all over again! For what feels like the fifty millionth time, the Yankees celebrated in Minnesota, as they clinched a postseason berth earlier this week with a victory over their favorite AL Central punching bag.
The Roberto Clemente Award
This week, the New York Yankees named Carlos Rodón their nominee for the 2026 Roberto Clemente Award. The team honored the Rodón Foundation, which sets out to help families suffering with fertility issues.
In Service
Yankees reliever Brent Headrick welcomed Henry Ledlowe from his hometown in Illinois to the Bronx, courtesy of the National Down Syndrome Society. Unfortunately, the Instagram post cannot be embedded, but can be found here.
The Jazz Chisholm Jr. Foundation, meanwhile, marked the 25th anniversary of 9/11.
Where’s Oswaldo? Unfortunately, Cincy.
This week, the Yankees designated fan favorite Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment in order to make room on the 40-man roster for Clarke Schmidt. Unfortunately, he was claimed off waivers by the Cincinnati Reds, and while we’re all excited to see him (hopefully) get some regular playing time — as he was very much blocked in the Bronx — it will be sad to see the human golden retriever, well-loved by the fans and players alike, in a different uniform.
A testament to his popularity is the fact that the Yankees, RailRiders, Patriots, and YES Network all posted farewells to him on their social media accounts. David Cone also came back to Twitter briefly in order to wish him well.
Farewell to the RailRiders
Starting next year, the Yankees’ Triple-A affiliate will undergo its second rebrand since joining the Yankees family, abandoning the RailRider moniker in exchange for a new nickname which has yet to be revealed. To honor the end of the era, Clint Frazier — who self-identifies as a Scranton RailRider more than anyone else in baseball — threw out the ceremonial first pitch prior to their final game.
Road Trip Nonsense
Meredith Marakovitz, Suzyn Waldman, and Dave Simms always have fun on the road trips, and this one is no different!
The Knicks are Back
This week, the Yankees will be hosting Josh Hart bobblehead night, celebrating the 2026 NBA Champion (and 2016 NCAA Champion!) who is related to Yankees legend Elston Howard. Fun fact — this has been scheduled since last year, so it actually predates the Knicks’ championship; what fantastic luck for the marketing team!
Celebrating Howie
Last Sunday, Mets broadcaster Howie Rose called his last game at Yankee Stadium. The Yankees set out to make the day special, and many of his friends and coworkers in the Yankees broadcast teams celebrated his career with him.
Official Videos
First, the latest episode of Behind the NY gives us a behind-the scenes look at the 25th anniversary of 9/11.
Then, we got a behind-the-scenes look of David Bednar entering the game on Sunday.
Last, but not least, we have Cody Bellinger talking about his story.
We’ve got a special edition of this week’s Question of the Day, as we not only have the Yankees answering questions, we’ve got the Somerset Patriots reading Thank You Cards as they wrap up their season.

PHOENIX — Both the Yankees and Rays saw their respective games end in walk-off fashion on Saturday, but only one of the division rivals emerged victorious.
It wasn’t the Yanks, who suffered a 5-3 loss to the Diamondbacks when Michael Fulmer surrendered a game-ending, two-run home to Pavin Smith with one out in the ninth inning. Aaron Boone said that he considered using Clarke Schmidt, one game back from Tommy John surgery, instead, but he went with the journeyman Fulmer because he’s had more experience in those situations.
“I just felt like Fulmer’s been in these spots and throwing the ball really well for us, and Smith got him there,” Boone said of the reliever, who has a 3.09 ERA this season.
Meanwhile, at Tropicana Field, the Rays pulled off a 2-1 win over the Red Sox thanks to a bloop single from Richie Palacios in the ninth. Tampa now has a five-game lead over the Yankees with just eight games left in the regular season.
The American League East foes will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium from Sept. 22-24, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday. Boone acknowledged that his club will probably have to sweep the Rays for a crack at a division title.
“We sweep, then it gets interesting,” the manager said with the Yankees’ postseason ticket already punched.
But the odds are already stacked against the Yankees with the team finishing its series in Arizona on Sunday. They entered Saturday with a just a 2.8% chance of winning the division, according to FanGraphs.
Making matters tougher is that the Rays, owners of the AL’s best record, currently lead the season series between the two teams, 6-3. There’s also the fact that the Yankees will be without Aaron Judge, who returned to the injured list with calf strain on Saturday.
“They’re playing tremendous baseball, so it’s tough to climb up in the standings when they keep winning,” Cody Bellinger said after going 0-for-4 on Saturday. “So mathematically, it’s pretty tough, but gotta keep on rolling.”
“We gotta go on a good run. It’s gonna be tough,” added Cam Schlittler, who allowed one earned run over six innings but committed a costly error on Saturday. “I think we’ve had opportunities all season to put ourselves ahead, and we haven’t done a great job with it. So there’s still a chance, but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
The good news for the Yankees is that their best starters are lined up to face the Rays. While they haven’t officially announced their probables for the series, it looks like Max Fried and Carlos Rodón will pitch the doubleheader before Gerrit Cole and Schlittler, the Cy Young frontrunner, close out the four-game set.
The Rays, however, are set to throw a few of their best with Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez, Ian Seymour and Freddy Peralta slotted for the highly-anticipated matchup.
While they’re not officially out of the division race yet, the likeliest scenario is that the Yankees end up hosting Boston in the Wild Card round for the second straight year. It is not where the team wants to end up after finishing 2025 with the same record as the Blue Jays but losing the season series tiebreaker, but Bellinger remained confident that the Yankees can still win their first title since 2009.
“Obviously, the goal is to win the division, rest your guys, get those extra off days,” he said. “That’s always goal No. 1. Ultimately, World Series champions have come out of the Wild Card.”

MLB Trade Rumors | Darragh McDonald: Well, it was nice while it lasted. The Yankees announced yesterday evening that they will be placing right fielder Aaron Judge on the ten-day injured list with a calf strain today; Max Schuemann is expected to be the corresponding move. Since it will be backdated to the 16th, Judge will be eligible to come off the IL for the final day of the season; however, given the nature of calf strains, it is entirely possible that we have seen the last of No. 99 for 2026.
New York Daily News | Gary Phillips: Arguably the biggest surprise of the 2026 season — beyond the fact that the Yankees somehow managed to keep their heads above water despite Aaron Judge missing three months, of course — has been the breakout of outfielder Spencer Jones. The former top prospect has managed to position himself as “a key cog in the Yankees’ lineup,” taking advantage of opportunities offered by injuries to Judge, Trent Grisham, Cody Bellinger, and Giancarlo Stanton. In particular, his performance against southpaws, which had long been a weakness throughout his minor league career, has been a pleasant surprise. That being said, it hasn’t been all sunshine and roses: Jones has yet to flash the leather in the way many have expected him to. Even so, however, it seems likely that Jones will be a critical part of the team’s postseason run, whether as the starting center fielder or a key reserve.
MLB.com | Mike Lupica: For all the attention that the Yankees’ veteran stars — Judge, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, and Giancarlo Stanton — receive, the 2026 season has been a veritable youth movement. Key to that has been the development, of course, of first baseman/designated hitter Ben Rice and AL Cy Young frontrunner Cam Schlittler. The two youngsters from Massachusetts, never highly rated as prospects, have turned themselves into veritable forces at the plate and on the mound, and without their contributions, the injury-riddled 2026 Yankees would almost certainly be spending the final few days of the season playing out the string, not attempting to make a last-ditch run at the AL East while lining up the rotation for a matchup with the Red Sox in the Wild Card round.
MLB Trade Rumors | Darragh McDonald: Yesterday afternoon, the Yankees announced that Oswaldo Cabrera, the popular utilityman who has been with the organization since 2015, had been claimed off waivers by the Cincinnati Reds. He had been designated for assignment earlier in the week, in order to make room on the 40-man roster for Clarke Schmidt.
Playbill | Logan Culwell-Block: Earlier this summer, former Mets infielder José Iglesias made the jump from the ballfield to the stage, joining the Broadway production of Buena Vista Social Club. Now, a Yankee great will be joining him: yesterday, Bernie Williams announced that he will be joining the show’s pit band for a limited run, from October 22nd through November 29th.

The New York Yankees could make a surprising move on Anthony Volpe.
Volpe has had success since being recalled, but George Lombard Jr. has taken over as the starting shortstop. So, Volpe's future in New York is very much up in the air.
New York will begin a three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday.
New York Yankees Surprise Anthony Volpe Decision
Although Volpe has been playing better, he isn't guaranteed a spot on the Yankees playoff roster.
After New York clinched a playoff spot, Yankees analysts Bryan Hoch and Patrick Donnelly of MLB.com revealed the likely playoff roster, and they didn't have Volpe on it.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez
1B: Luis García Jr., Paul Goldschmidt
2B: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
3B: Ryan McMahon, Amed Rosario
SS: George Lombard Jr., José Caballero
OF: Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Aaron Judge, Heliot Ramos
DH: Ben Rice
SP: Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole
RP: David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Tim Hill, Ryan Yarbrough, Clarke Schmidt, Michael Fulmer, Ryan Weathers, Will Warren
The Yankees leaving Volpe off the playoff roster would be a disappointing outcome for the shortstop. It also could signal the end of his tenure in New York as Lombard is the shortstop of the future.
Volpe is hitting .253 with 2 home runs and 26 RBIs this season with the Yankees.
New York Right Now
The Yankees have clinched a playoff spot as New York will be hosting a Wild Card series again.
"Every year you go through a lot, it seems like. But we've been through a lot this year with injuries, with adversity," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. "But credit to them for coming together. Through all the ups and downs, they've been a together group. I feel like they've developed a lot of grit over the season."
However, despite clinching a playoff spot, the Yankees made it clear the job isn't finished. New York likely won't win the AL East again, which is frustrating, but the Yankees have confidence they can go on a deep playoff run.
The Yankees are 88-64 and 5 games back of the Tampa Bay Rays for the top spot in the AL East.

With Clarke Schmidt being activated off the 60-day IL as he returns from Tommy John surgery, the Yankees are creating room on the 40-man roster by designating utility player Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment.
Cabrera was then claimed by the Cincinnati Reds, ending his time with the Yankee organization after five seasons in The Bronx.
Cabrera played just three games for the Yanks this season as he spent the majority of the year with Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes Barre, where he was hitting .288/.345/.444 in 122 games while getting starts at all four infield positions and both corner outfield spots.
The 27-year-old appeared in 304 games at the big league level, posting a .232/.292/.343 slash line for a .635 OPS. In 15 postseason games, Cabrera tallied three hits in 34 at-bats with a .420 OPS.
As for Schmidt, he has been out since July 3 of last season, when he was diagnosed with a torn UCL that required Tommy John surgery that also included an internal brace procedure.
Schmidt had a 3.32 ERA (3.95 FIP) and 1.09 WHIP in 14 starts last season before going down with his injury.
In another notable move on Wednesday, hard-throwing pitching prospect Carlos Lagrange was activated off the IL in Triple-A.
Lagrange, who had been dealing with a right shoulder sprain, last pitched on June 28.

It wasn't all bad news from a discouraging and frustrating 13-inning defeat at the hands of the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday afternoon, even if it really, really stung for a number of reasons.
The ray of sunshine in what was a rough day for the Yankees' divisional hopes was the return of someone they view as crucial to their chances at a deep playoff run. After a 440-day absence due to Tommy John surgery, Clarke Schmidt made his Yankees return, tossing two-thirds of an inning in the seventh before being removed due to pitch count.
It wasn't the cleanest outing, as he wasn't able to get through a full inning after throwing 24 pitches to four batters, but for someone on a big league mound for the first time in 14 months, you had to like what you saw, striking out a pair and only surrendering a pair of soft-hit singles.
The runway is rather short for the remainder of the season with just 10 games left, but Schmidt will likely see his way into four or so games down the stretch. That gives him a total of five outings to truly figure out where he can fit into a wide-open bullpen trust tree.
Clarke Schmidt's bullpen experience
Converting a full-time starter to the bullpen is not always as easy as it seems, but it's a transition the Yankees will have to make three times as we head into the postseason, with Ryan Weathers' likely return and Will Warren's place in the rotation. That said, Schmidt has a bit of an advantage.
Before becoming a full-time starter at the major-league level in 2023, Schmidt was used almost exclusively as a reliever in his brief big-league stints, most notably in 2022, when he posted a 3.12 ERA in 57.2 innings as part of a makeshift bullpen that got very good results. He didn't get himself high up the totem pole, but he pitched some important innings for the club.
His playoff experience as a reliever was unfortunately one to forget. He was saddled with a pair of losses, first in Game 3 of the ALDS after a squeaker by Oscar Gonzalez got through the infield for a walk-off single, and the second in Game 1 of the ALCS against the Houston Astros, where he allowed home runs to Yuli Gurriel and Chas McCormick in the sixth inning of what would be the start of a sweep.
He was supposed to be in the bullpen the following season, but a mountain of injuries forced him to step up in the rotation, starting what became a nightmarish 2023 season. Since then, Schmidt has made 63 appearances through his season-ending elbow surgery in 2025, all but one as a starter.
That's not in the cards for 2026, so what can he do to be useful for the Yankees in the playoffs?
Where Schmidt could fit into unstable bullpen
Schmidt adds a multi-inning righty option to a bullpen that has a lot of moving parts. He leaned hard on a cutter-slider combo on Wednesday, but also featured his sinker, four-seamer, and curveball. His velocity looked as firm as ever, something that could be enhanced but didn't need to hold back for 100 pitches.
The bullpen's premier multi-inning righty is Paul Blackburn, who relies on a ton of spin and movement in his profile, making him more volatile in games with shoddy command. He, along with closer David Bednar and lefty Brent Headrick, makes up the team's three highest-leverage arms, but it's wide open beneath them, particularly after Fernando Cruz's elbow injury.
John Schreiber has been effective as a righty specialist in a small sample, so he feels like the leader in the clubhouse as the team's sixth-inning arm, but he might not be playable in certain matchups due to his struggles against lefties. Tim Hill's overall struggles, even if he remains sharp against lefties, will also give pause. Michael Fulmer and Luis Gil haven't pitched enough to earn trust in leverage.
There are two ways that Schmidt can be deployed. One of which is as the team's right-handed bridge reliever, as sort of a "platoon" with Ryan Yarbrough (or Weathers, when he returns). Lineups with more right-handed hitters will fare significantly better against Weathers or Yarbrough if the team needs them to come into a big spot to provide some length to the back-end guys, so having a guy with the opposite hand who can fill that role is valuable.
But that role could be reserved for Warren, who's more stretched out than Schmidt and isn't at risk of being removed due to a long inning. I doubt Schmidt would be permitted to throw much more than 30 pitches in a game. That could lead the 30-year-old to be more in the Schreiber role as the sixth-inning guy, possibly pitching in higher leverage if needed due to overuse.
There are a lot of questions about Schmidt as we come down the stretch, but the important thing is that he's back and he's healthy. The more bullpen depth, the merrier.

Pitching has been a major strength for the New York Yankees this season, particularly starting pitching. But the Yankees have dealt with numerous pitching injuries with Max Fried (two stints on the IL), Carlos Rodón (two stints on the IL), Ryan Weathers (currently on the IL) and Fernando Cruz (currently on the IL) all going down at certain points of the season. Not to mention, Gerrit Cole and Clarke Schmidt missed time this year while recovering from Tommy John surgery, and Rodón didn't make his season debut until May due to offseason surgery.
So it remains to be seen whether the Yankees' pitching staff will be able to hold up for a deep postseason run. And on Wednesday against the Minnesota Twins, Rodón initially gave Yankees fans cause for concern.
Rodón's concerning dip in velocity vs. Twins
Rodón's fastball velocity was down in the low-90s across the first three innings of his most recent start in Minnesota. The left-hander threw some fastballs at 90 mph to begin the game and averaged 92.6 mph on the pitch, as opposed to his season average of 94.4 mph.
Luckily, Rodón was able to crank things up in his final three innings of work, throwing a number of pitches above 95 mph afterwards. This likely made the Yankees and their fans breathe a sigh of relief for the time being. But Rodón's explanation after the game won't give fans much clarity.
Rodón's explanation
According to Gary Phillips of The New York Daily News, Rodón told reporters that he was dealing with tightness at the beginning of his start, but was able to get loose as his outing progressed. Rodón didn't specify where he was feeling tight/whether it was localized or if he was just trying to say he felt a generalized sense that he couldn't break through the way he wanted to.
So while it's good news that Rodón was able to shake it off after the third, the Yankees should still be worried about his overall durability with the postseason around the corner. Rodón is slated to be the Yankees' No. 4 starter in the playoffs behind Cam Schlittler, Cole and Fried. They will have to hope that his tightness doesn't come back in his next start or in the postseason or snowball into something worse.
As aforementioned, Rodón was out until May of this season after undergoing surgery to remove a bone spur from his left elbow last October. He also dealt with a hamstring issue during his rehab. In addition to his initial IL stint, Rodón missed over a month and a half of action from Jun. 28 to Aug. 18 with left elbow inflammation. The 33-year-old has pitched very well in 15 starts this season (2.95 ERA), but this latest blip should have the Yankees questioning whether they can rely on him the rest of the way.

Yankees Urged to Leave Luis Gil Off Playoff Roster

"But for now, Gil is on the roster bubble, and we don't expect him to crack the 26-man playoff squad. That said, we imagine he'd be among the first names called if injuries strike his teammates. "

What Has Luis Gil Done in His MLB Career
Luis Gil has technically pitched in five seasons with the New York Yankees.
He briefly pitched in 2021 and 2022 with the club, but did not pitch at all in MLB in 2023 before bursting onto the scene in 2024 (AL Rookie of the Year).
However, since earning that top accolade, he has not been consistent as a member in the Yankees rotation.
Across 265.1 total IP in his career, Gil holds a very respectable 3.66 ERA, but perhaps his absence from the Bigs is a product of the Yankees' loaded rotation, rather than his individual ability.

On the offensive front, the New York Yankees have a lot to worry about. Pitching-wise, things are okay — more than okay, actually.
Despite a lackluster trade deadline in which general manager Brian Cashman failed to add any relievers, the team bolstered its pitching depth in the weeks that followed. They lucked out by adding John Schreiber, which was essentially a salary dump for the Kansas City Royals, and Clarke Schmidt coming off the IL is another positive.
The Yankees' 5-4 loss to the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday afternoon was an ugly one they needed, and Minnesota's walk-off left a bad taste, while Aaron Judge had another injury scare. But it was another stellar day for the pen, outside of David Bednar letting up two leads in extras. Schmidt is one reason to look forward to what the pen could be in October, and even if he has a little more rust to knock off, there are a few things to be excited about.
Giving length
Schmidt isn't built up, but he should be good to give a little more than an inning at a time as a reliever. While he only pitched 2/3 innings in his return to the mound, it's clear the Yankees are building Schmidt up to go multiple innings. In three of his five rehab starts, he pitched more than one inning. In two of them, he pitched two innings.
Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick have clearly been overworked. Somebody like Schmidt lightens their load, and soon another starter, Ryan Weathers, will join the bullpen.
More strikeout stuff in the bullpen
The Yankees have desperately needed strikeout stuff, especially in the middle innings. The Yankees have guys who can generate whiffs in Bednar, Blackburn, and Headrick, but that's missing if a starter comes out early. Schmidt gives them that. He struck out two batters in his debut, and despite allowing two hits, he navigated through it because of the whiffs.
Schmidt also showed strikeout stuff in his rehab start. He struck out 11 batters in seven innings. He hasn't had a full season since 2023, but in 2024 and 2025 combined, the veteran hurler had a 9.11 K/9. That should play in October.
No more sweeper?
The sweeper was Schmidt's second-most-used pitch in 2024. It was his third-most-used pitch in 2023. Against the Minnesota Twins, he didn't throw it once. It could be a pitch he's throwing away.
It would be a surprise if he did that, though. Batters hit .210 off it and struck out 33.8% of the time against it in 2024. In 2025, they hit .125 off the sweeper. They struck out 35.8% of the time against it. It's something to look to in future outings.
Potential trade bait
You can never have too much pitching, and if there is one thing the 2026 Yankees understand full well, it's that pitching depth is paramount. It's how they navigated the season.
That said, Schmidt has one year left after this season. The Yankees may want to sell high on him if they don't plan on bringing him back. The rotation should be full again next year, and if they need pitching depth, they have Ryan Weathers and Will Warren.
This season could be a showcase of sorts for Schmidt. The veteran showing he can finish out the season could be a selling point in the winter.
Chances are, Schmidt won't be able to start next year anyway, and if he does, he won't have a full workload since he needs to build back up. The last time he pitched more than 150 innings was in 2023. That said, the Yankees could use this as an opportunity to deal an oft-injured pitcher and fill another area of need.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

MINNEAPOLIS — La primera mañana de Clarke Schmidtde vuelta en la plantilla de los Yankees empezó con una pequeña petición, tras más de 14 meses alejado del montículo de las Grandes Ligas. Quería un café, a ser posible un café con leche, antes de su tan esperado regreso el miércoles en el Target Field.
El lanzador diestro ya tenía la adrenalina a tope. Schmidt entró en el partido que los Yankees perdieron por 5-4 en la 13.ª entrada ante los Twins como primer relevo tras Carlos Rodón, tomando el relevo en la séptima entrada con Nueva York perdiendo por 2-0. Era su primera aparición en las Grandes Ligas desde el 3 de julio de 2025.
Schmidt consiguió dos outs, ponchó a dos y permitió dos sencillos flojos en 24 lanzamientos, 13 de ellos strikes. Su bola rápida de cuatro costuras alcanzó las 95,8 mph. Brent Headrick dejó a ambos corredores heredados en base antes de que los Yankees empataran el partido en la novena entrada con un doble de dos carreras de Anthony Volpe.
Para Schmidt, esa entrada tuvo más importancia que una simple salida como relevo. Dijo que su regreso fue muy emotivo tras someterse a una segunda operación de Tommy John y a una rehabilitación llena de días monótonos lejos de la competición. Su padre, Dwight, piloto de Delta Air Lines, se reorganizó la agenda para estar en Minnesota.
«Se parece mucho a tu debut», dijo Schmidt. «Por suerte, ahora me siento un poco más a gusto, pero creo que las emociones eran parecidas y sentí la misma descarga de adrenalina».
Los Yankees también pudieron comprobar de inmediato las limitaciones de su papel actual. Schmidt está lanzando desde el bullpen porque no hubo tiempo suficiente para prepararlo como titular antes de que termine la temporada regular. No le gustó nada haber llegado a tres cuentas de tres bolas contra cuatro bateadores, aunque los golpes que recibió fueron débiles.
Esa salida demostró que su brazo está respondiendo. Para los Yankees, que están evaluando todas las opciones para el bullpen de la postemporada, las próximas salidas servirán para ver si Schmidt es capaz de controlar sus lanzamientos bajo mayor presión y recuperarse siguiendo el ritmo de un relevista en octubre.
Schmidt vuelve sin uno de sus lanzamientos estrella
Schmidt confirmó el jueves que ya no lanza su «sweeper», un lanzamiento que, según él, contribuyó a los problemas en el codo que le llevaron a someterse a una cirugía de Tommy John tras terminar la temporada de 2025.
Él y el departamento de pitcheo de los Yankees modificaron el agarre durante la temporada 2025 para conseguir un movimiento más horizontal. Schmidt empezó a usar esa versión el 6 de mayo contra San Diego. Más tarde comentó que ese agarre requería más presión y fuerza de giro. Un mes después, unas molestias en el antebrazo derecho complicaron su recuperación entre salidas.
«Creo que lo que más influyó fueron los cambios de empuñadura a mitad de temporada», dijo Schmidt en marzo. «Cuando cambias de empuñadura, empiezas a ejercer una tensión diferente en distintas zonas del antebrazo y cosas así».
La propuesta había funcionado, lo que complicaba la decisión de descartarla.
«Estaba consiguiendo muy buenos resultados con eso, así que es difícil decir: “Vale, dejemos de lanzarlo”», dijo Schmidt. «Era como un arma de doble filo».
Cuánto cuesta realmente perder al líbero
Los datos de Statcast de 2025 muestran que Schmidt lanzó el «sweeper» el 12,2 % de las veces. Los bateadores tuvieron un promedio de bateo de 0,125 contra él, con un wOBA de 0,188, y generó una tasa de strikes fallidos del 35,8 %.
Los Yankees no necesitan necesariamente un sustituto que lo iguale en todo. El slider de Schmidt dio mejores resultados en cuanto a valor de carrera en 2025. Los rivales batearon .061 contra él, con un wOBA de .139, y ese lanzamiento valió siete carreras, frente a la única del «sweeper».
Su uso de lanzamientos ya había bajado desde el 23,7 % registrado en 2024. El miércoles lanzó cinco tipos de lanzamientos: bola rápida de cuatro costuras, cutter, slider, sinker y curva de nudillos.
Esa combinación les da a los Yankees varias rangos de velocidad y perfiles de movimiento sin tener que volver al agarre que, según Schmidt, le causaba tensión en el brazo.
Los Yankees muestran serenidad, pero aún tienen que pulir la ejecución
A Aaron Boone le gustó cómo se las apañó Schmidt en un partido reñido tras una ausencia tan larga, aunque dos lanzamientos mal colocados acabaran en sencillos.
«Se le veía muy en forma y no parecía nada agobiado ni con prisas», dijo Boone. «Es un partido reñido, tu primer partido en más de un año, y seguro que hay algo de nerviosismo. Creo que lo ha gestionado bastante bien. Con suerte, a medida que vaya jugando, irá cogiendo un poco más de ritmo».
Schmidt también se enfrentó al ritmo poco habitual del papel de relevo. Empezó a calentar en la primera entrada, cuando Rodón tenía dificultades, y luego tuvo que sentarse y esperar hasta la séptima.
«Como suele pasar en el bullpen, me dieron un poco de caña en la primera entrada», dijo Schmidt riéndose. «Pensé que Carlos iba a salir, estaba emocionado y la adrenalina me subía por las nubes. Y luego tuve que volver a sentarme y calmarme un momento».
Las pruebas de octubre pasan de la recuperación al repertorio
Los Yankees han dado de alta a Schmidt tras cinco partidos de rehabilitación en las ligas menores, en los que cedió tres carreras en siete entradas, ponchó a 11 y concedió una base por bolas. No lanzará dos días seguidos, y Boone ha dicho que podría hacer más de tres outs dependiendo de cómo vaya la recuperación.
La temporada 2025 de Schmidt había ido muy bien antes de la lesión. Acumuló un balance de 4-4 con una efectividad de 3,32 en 14 salidas como titular, mantuvo a sus rivales en un promedio de bateo de 0,199 y encadenó una racha de 28 1/3 entradas sin encajar carreras en junio.
Ahora los Yankees están evaluando algo diferente. En su primera noche tras el regreso, mostró una velocidad de unos 90, dos strikeouts por swing y la compostura suficiente para afrontar un regreso lleno de adrenalina. El lanzamiento «sweeper» ya no está, y los Yankees necesitan ver si el resto del arsenal de Schmidt puede asumir la carga de trabajo que antes ayudaba a llevar ese lanzamiento.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario abajo.

For their sake, the New York Yankees better hope that superstar outfielder Aaron Judge’s newest injury is only a minor setback.
Judge left Wednesday’s extra-inning loss to the Twins with lower leg tightness, immediately raising concerns among fans that he’ll miss the Yankees’ first playoff series. New York entered play on Sept. 17 in firm control of the AL’s top Wild Card seed, putting them on track to host the No. 5 Red Sox in the first round.
If Judge can’t go when the playoffs begin on Sept. 29, then he won’t be the only notable contributor not in uniform during the Wild Card Series. Each team gets 26 players for their playoff rosters, but no more than 13 pitchers. Some clubs opt for 14 position players and 12 pitchers, though we personally prefer a 13-and-13 balance. Additionally, teams can adjust their rosters between series, and obviously they can replace an injured player if needed.
For this list, we’re only including players who are healthy and active as of Sept. 17. In other words, that means Trent Grisham, Giancarlo Stanton, and Ryan Weathers are among those who didn’t qualify. We’ve also omitted Judge because the Yankees haven’t announced the severity of his left leg injury.
Jasson Domínguez, OF
The writing has long been on the wall for Domínguez, who was recently demoted to Triple-A amid another disappointing season. Even if Judge potentially misses the Wild Card Round, it’s difficult to envision the 23-year-old Domínguez returning as a backup outfielder.
Frankly, the entire situation is unfortunate, because neither Domínguez’s talent nor his work ethic has been the issue. He’s always earned rave reviews for his maturity and overall attitude, but injuries — most notably to his elbow and shoulder — have seemingly sapped him of his once-potent power stroke.
Luis Gil, P
Gil has had an odd career, winning AL Rookie of the Year in 2024 despite debuting three years earlier. Injuries have limited him to a 3.92 ERA over 80.1 innings since the start of 2025, and he recently moved to the bullpen. We’ll see whether the Yankees view the 28-year-old as a long-term reliever, or if they’d bring him to spring training as a starter.
But for now, Gil is on the roster bubble, and we don’t expect him to crack the 26-man playoff squad. Clarke Schmidt’s return gives the Yankees another depth arm, and Gil hasn’t shown that he’s worth carrying on a limited staff. That said, we imagine he’d be among the first names called if injuries strike his teammates.
Paul Goldschmidt, 1B/DH
Goldschmidt turned 39 last week, and it’s unclear whether he’s in the final weeks of a likely Hall of Fame career. He’s totaled 65.3 bWAR, and the majority of the 142 players above him are already in the Hall of Fame or will be when they’re eligible.
Let’s get back to the present. Goldschmidt is hitting just .239 with a .680 OPS in 103 second-half plate appearances, and he’s only capable of playing first or DHing. Ben Rice fills both roles, and Cody Bellinger can also play first if needed.
The one thing potentially working in Goldschmidt’s favor is his .313 average and 1.006 OPS against lefties, but that’s not enough to warrant a roster spot in our eyes. Sorry, Goldy. At least you’d finally earn a World Series ring if the Yankees finish the job.
Will Warren, SP
This might come as a surprise, given that we included Warren in our most recent playoff roster projection. But the more that we think about things, Schmidt’s return feels like a significant blow to Warren’s chances of pitching in October. Do the Yankees really need two long relievers capable of eating up innings if the starter leaves early?
We initially had veteran swingman Ryan Yarbrough in this spot, though he might have the advantage as a left-handed reliever.. He also has a 2.91 ERA in 21.2 second-half innings and has since recovered from a lingering right oblique problem.

MINNESOTA — Fresh off the injured list in time for a morning report to the visitor’s clubhouse at Target Field, Clarke Schmidt searched for a pick-me-up on Wednesday.
The Yankees’ pitcher, eagerly anticipating his long-awaited return from Tommy John surgery, wanted nothing more than to take the mound later in the day. But first, he craved a cup of coffee. A latte, preferably.
And if he couldn’t find one?
“Day over,” Schmidt joked. “Not activated.”
It turns out that Schmidt didn’t really need the caffeine, as he was plenty amped up by the time he was summed into the Yankees’ 13-inning, 5-4 loss to the Twins. The first man out of the bullpen — the starter is working as a reliever since he didn’t have time to build up — Schmidt took over for Carlos Rodón with the Bombers down 2-0 in the seventh inning.
It was his first appearance since July 3, 2025.
“It’s a lot like your debut,” Schmidt said. “Thankfully, I’m a little bit more comfortable now, but I think it was similar emotions and a surge of adrenaline.”
Schmidt added that entering the game was “emotional,” and that he had to focus on staying present and slowing things down as he exited the bullpen.
“He looked pretty sharp and didn’t look sped up or overwhelmed at all,” Aaron Boone said. “It’s a tight ballgame there, your first game in over a year, and I’m sure there’s some emotions there. I thought he handled all that pretty well. Hopefully, as he goes now, he’ll get a little sharper.”
That’s not to say that Schmidt didn’t flash potential with the Yankees hoping he can factor into their postseason bullpen. He and Boone were happy with the right-hander’s stuff, and the fact that Schmidt got two swinging strikeouts.
His velocity, meanwhile, topped out at 95.8 mph over 24 pitches.
But Schmidt only got two outs and had to be relieved by Brent Headrick, who got out of the inning unscathed, after allowing two singles. Each knock came on weak contact, but Boone also felt Schmidt’s execution on those pitches could have been better.
Schmidt, meanwhile, was frustrated that he got into three three-ball counts over four batters faced.
Still, the 30-year-old was happy to be an active pitcher again, even if that meant prematurely warming up during a rocky first inning for Rodón.
“In traditional bullpen fashion, I got dry humped a little bit in the first,” Schmidt said with a laugh. “I thought Carlos was coming out, and I was excited and the adrenaline was at a high. And then I had to sit back down and settle down for a second.”
Before and after Wednesday’s game, Schmidt took time to reflect on his long road back from his second Tommy John operation, which he called “not an easy journey at all.” The hardest part, he said, was spending so much time away from the game and a lot of “long, monotonous days” of rehab.
“It was almost like a zero dark thirty-type feel. It’s like you rinse, wash, repeat. You’re doing the same thing every single day,” Schmidt said. “It’s trying to get as much sleep as you can, showing up early in the morning and before the team’s there, and putting all the work in and then staying for the game.
“You learn a lot about yourself spiritually and how to continue to just keep going and keep being resilient.”
Schmidt noted that he leaned on his faith and family a lot to get through the grueling rehab process, so he appreciated that his father, Dwight, a pilot for Delta Air Lines, was able to rearrange his work schedule and make it to Minnesota on Wednesday.
“He’s a trooper, man,” Schmidt said. “[My family] always tries to have one family member at my outings. I’ve been so blessed and so lucky to have a family who’s supportive of me and has been with me every step of the way. I know I wouldn’t be where I’m at without them.”

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Anthony Volpe bateó con tanta fuerza que perdió el equilibrio, convencido de que la pelota se había ido fuera. En cambio, rebotó contra el muro alto del centro-derecha, un doble de dos carreras que igualó el marcador para los Yankees con dos outs en la novena entrada. Durante un momento intenso y emocionante el miércoles, Nueva York parecía dispuesta a llevarse la barrida.
Lo que vino después fueron cuatro entradas más en las que el equipo llegaba hasta la puerta y se negaba a cruzarla. Los Yankees se pusieron por delante en la décima. Volvieron a hacerlo en la undécima. Llenaron las bases sin outs en la duodécima. Cada vez acababan con un empate o con una remontada desperdiciada.
Un viaje que debería haber acabado con una barrida acabó poniendo de manifiesto el único punto débil que un aspirante al título no puede permitirse arrastrar hasta octubre. No se trató de un colapso del bullpen ni de un rebote desafortunado. Fue la alineación de los Yankees la que no paraba de preparar la mesa, pero nunca se sentaba a comer.
La culpa final recayó en un novato que no se la merecía él solo.
Los Minnesota Twins vencieron a los Yankees por 5-4 en 13 entradas, poniendo fin a ese partido maratoniano con un sencillo de Victor Caratini en la primera base que rebotó en el montículo y se coló por debajo del guante de George Lombard Jr. en la segunda base. Con esta derrota, Nueva York queda con un balance de 88-64, a cuatro partidos de los Rays de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, a falta de 10 partidos por disputar. Los Yankees ya tienen asegurada su plaza en los playoffs, pero el título de la división y la exención de la primera ronda se les están escapando.
Una remontada que no llevó a ninguna parte
Nueva York había sumado cuatro hits en ocho entradas y perdía por 2-0, mientras que el lanzador diestro de los Twins, Zebby Matthews, había ponchado a ocho. Entonces llegó la novena entrada. Lombard conectó un sencillo, Paul Goldschmidt le siguió y el corredor suplente José Caballero preparó el terreno para Volpe.
Volpe impulsó las dos carreras, lo que le supuso al cerrador de los Twins, Yoendrys Gómez, su primer salvamento fallido del año y obligó a jugar entradas extras.
Ali Sánchez impulsó al corredor automático con un sencillo en la décima entrada, dando a los Yankees su primera ventaja. Luke Keaschall respondió con un sencillo que empató el partido ante David Bednar. Un fly de sacrificio de Caballero puso a Nueva York por delante en la undécima. Royce Lewis igualó el marcador. Dos ventajas, dos respuestas inmediatas.
La entrada que dará que hablar
La 12.ª es la entrada que los aficionados volverán a ver una y otra vez. Los Yankees llenaron las bases sin outs, la situación que debería haber sentenciado el partido. Pero no sacaron nada de ella.
Heliot Ramos, que bateaba en el turno de Aaron Judge, mandó una bola corta hacia el montículo. Travis Adams la convirtió en una doble jugada 1-2-3. Sánchez se fue con un strikeout, dejando a otros dos en base. Los Yankees acabaron con 7 de 30 con corredores en posición de anotar.
El juez se marcha y el ataque se queda con pocos jugadores
Judge se retiró en la sexta entrada por una contractura en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha que empezó a notar en la primera entrada. Falló dos veces y no volvió al campo, solo siete partidos después de una ausencia de 99 días. Por eso Ramos estaba bateando en su lugar.
El entrenador Aaron Boone describió la noche como una oportunidad perdida, no como un partido robado, y sus palabras reflejaban la importancia del momento en el calendario.
«Obviamente, muchas cosas buenas, pero no las suficientes», dijo Boone. «Ha sido un golpe duro, claro, cuando tenías la oportunidad de barrer la serie y justo antes de un día de descanso. Pero tenemos que superarlo y prepararnos para enfrentarnos a un buen equipo de los Diamondbacks».
Al final del partido, Boone no se anduvo con rodeos con Lombard, pero tampoco lo machacó.
Boone reconoció que la bola de Caratini rebotó en el montículo, pero fue una jugada que Lombard «se espera que haga y sabemos que es capaz de hacer».
Rodón lo da todo en octubre, pero no saca nada a cambio
Carlos Rodón le dio a los Yankees el comienzo que necesita una rotación en la postemporada y vio cómo se esfumaba. El zurdo encajó dos carreras en seis entradas, ampliando su récord de la franquicia a 25 salidas consecutivas en las que ha encajado tres carreras o menos. Lanzó 102 lanzamientos, su máximo de la temporada, y bajó su promedio de carreras limpias a 2,95.
«Empecé un poco lento, un poco tenso», dijo Rodon. «Me fui soltando en las siguientes entradas, así que eso estuvo bien».
Clarke Schmidt hizo su tan esperado regreso en la séptima entrada, ponchando a dos antes de que Brent Headrick dejara a dos en base. El bullpen corrió una maratón que la alineación nunca supo recompensar.
Una primicia para el club que no se veía desde 1991
Este es el dato que pocos destacarán. Ha sido la primera derrota de los Yankees tras ir ganando varias veces en entradas extras desde el 5 de mayo de 1991, en Seattle, es decir, en un lapso de más de 34 años. También fue su octava derrota en la última entrada de la temporada, un récord de la franquicia, y ningún equipo de la MLB ha encajado más hits decisivos en la última entrada en 2026, según datos de Baseball Reference. Ningún equipo de los Yankees ha perdido nunca más partidos a domicilio en entradas extras en una sola temporada.
Lo curioso es que los equipos malos no acumulan cifras como estas. Un equipo mediocre pierde en nueve partidos. Solo un buen equipo es capaz de forzar una prórroga fuera de casa una y otra vez, y luego seguir perdiéndola.
Cómo queda la carrera por la División Este de la Liga Americana
Spencer Jones lanzó su propia advertencia, ponchándose cinco veces en una noche en la que se fue de 0 de 6, lo que demostró lo rápido que se castigan los swings fallidos cuando los márgenes se estrechan. En septiembre se lee de otra manera que en julio.
Los Yankees tienen el jueves libre antes de empezar una serie de fin de semana en Arizona, donde Gerrit Cole será el lanzador titular el viernes a las 21:40 h (hora del Este). No se espera que Judge tenga que hacerse más pruebas. Nueva York ha perdido terreno que quizá no recupere y le ha dado un respiro a los Rays.
Los Yankees saben cómo ganar los partidos intermedios. Una noche en la que solo tenían que ganar uno, no pudieron.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

Yahoo Sports: As you likely know by now, Aaron Judge exited yesterday's game early when Heliot Ramos pinch-hit for him in the sixth. The Yankees announced it midgame as "lower leg tightness." It's some relief I suppose that Judge didn't re-aggravate the rib fracture that kept him out for over three months, and Judge himself downplayed the seriousness of the ailment after the game.
"We're still trying to ramp up so there's still going to be little things like this that come up," Judge said after the Yankees 13-inning loss to the Twins. "I just thought it would be best instead of pushing through it like I normally do." Judge seemed to view his exit from the game as precautionary, and likened it to the type of thing that would happen in spring training when small, nagging things pop up as players get back into playing shape.
MLB.com | Patrick Donnelly: Clarke Schmidt came off the 60-day injured list yesterday, something we saw coming; he allowed two hits but got two strikeouts while facing four batters in his first MLB action since July 3, 2025. What we didn't see coming was who was pushed off the roster to make room for Schmidt: fan favorite Oswaldo Cabrera. The utilityman Cabrera had spent most of the year at Triple-A, hitting .288 with 19 homers and a .790 OPS, but hasn't spent much time with the big club ever since suffering a brutal ankle injury in a play at home plate last May. Cabrera seems likely to be claimed on waivers, meaning his time in the Bronx is likely to come to an end after being a member of the organization since signing at age-16 in July 2015.
The Athletic | Brendan Kuty: ($) Spencer Jones has been a bit of a revelation for the Yankees this year, producing at a high level across the outfield throughout the summer. He's benefited from shadowing another big lefty swinger in the outfield: Cody Bellinger. Bellinger is only 31, but has a very long and decorated track record for a player his age, something Jones has tried to tap into during his time with the Yankees. "As a young guy, I can't help but watch every time he's up there," Jones said of Bellinger. "When we are in the dugout," Jones said, "he's one of those people I can go up to and ask, like, 'Yo, what did you see?' He'll tell me bluntly what he saw, how he saw it, and essentially what he's going to do next time."
New York Daily News | Gary Phillips: Ryan Weathers cleared a key hurdle in his rehab earlier this week, tossing 15 pitches in a bullpen session and sitting 87-90 mph on his fastball. The hope, if things go right, is for the lefty to get into game action before the regular season ends. It's a tight timeline, but with Weathers set to throw another bullpen on Friday before perhaps facing live hitters early next week, it's doable. The Yankees could certainly use his arm in the bullpen as they try to sort out what their playoff relief corps will look like.
FanGraphs | Davy Andrews: This here isn't news, but it is fun. Andrews discusses the Amazon TV show Reacher, in which the titular character tries to maintain a low profile by checking into hotels under aliases, which are always Yankees second basemen. The problem, of course, is that Reacher's cover is often blown, because Yankee second basemen are frequently famous people with recognizable names (don't choose "Starlin Castro" as your alias if you're trying not to attract attention!). So, Andrews endeavors to help Reacher by finding players who played second base for the Yankees who would help Reacher stay undercover. Good aliases include second basemen from New York's Higlander days, like Joe Ward, and Otis Johnson. The worst possible aliases Andrews found? Robinson Canó and Mickey Mantle.

Assuming Trent Grisham is healthy, who starts in center field during the playoffs: him or Spencer Jones? — Ed H.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Wednesday that Grisham is running “up to a decent speed” in his comeback from a right hamstring strain. Considering Grisham at normal speed is slow, it’s anyone’s guess what that actually means.
If Grisham is ready to go, it will be interesting to see what Boone decides. There are numerous examples of the Yankees opting for the veteran over an inexperienced player like Jones when the games matter most.
Both players have their warts. Neither Grisham nor Jones is a good defensive center fielder. Jones looked abysmal in center, letting a ground ball go under his glove, dropping a fly ball that hit his glove and nearly trucking Heliot Ramos in right field. Meanwhile, Grisham has trouble getting to balls over his head and in the gaps because he’s slow-footed. There’s likely a higher floor of success, though, for Grisham. Even on the balls Jones has caught, there have been instances where he doesn’t look comfortable reading the play off the bat.
So the main difference will come down to offense.
Before Grisham injured his hamstring, he was not hitting. Calls for Jones to take over were already happening. To Jones’ credit, he has produced at the plate. Even after a dreadful 0-for-6 performance with five strikeouts on Wednesday, Jones has a 113 wRC+. He is always a threat to pop a home run, and that wins ballgames in October.
Grisham has one of the best eyes on the team, rarely strikes out and works at-bats. That matters when the batters behind him would likely be Ben Rice and Judge (depending on his health).
Not that my opinion holds any weight, but I’d stick with Jones in center field. The Yankees can always use Grisham, who’s one of the most clutch hitters on the team, in big spots off the bench.

What will/should the Yankees playoff rotation and bullpen look like? I hate to say it, but Gerrit Cole and Max Fried are not looking like aces these days. The team is winning Will Warren’s and Carlos Rodón’s starts. How are these facts likely to influence Boone’s postseason rotation decisions? … As soon as I say this, Fried pitches a gem. Jinx. — Aaron D.
The American League East race isn’t over yet, but the likeliest outcome is the Yankees will play in a wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox. That means the Yankees will only need three starting pitchers for the first round.
Cam Schlittler should start Game 1. There’s no argument otherwise. Schlittler is one of the very best starting pitchers in the sport. You want your best pitcher going in Game 1 to give yourself the best possible chance of not facing a must-win Game 2.
From there, it’ll be a toss-up between Fried and Cole. Both pitchers have concerns attached to them.
Fried has battled command issues all season, while Cole has allowed plenty of hard contact while not getting much swing-and-miss. I’d lean toward Fried over Cole.
As for the bullpen, the Yankees could have Rodón in case the club needs length. The others likely to be on the roster are Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, John Schreiber, Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Yarbrough and Ryan Weathers, if he’s healthy. I’d leave off Tim Hill, who has struggled mightily this season, Luis Gil and Michael Fulmer.
What is the realistic outlook for second base next year? Jazz Chisholm Jr. hasn’t played up to his talent, which might make him more enticing by bringing down his cost. The infield is already crowded, though, with Ryan McMahon under contract, George Lombard Jr.’s promotion, José Caballero, two first basemen (three if Paul Goldschmidt is still seen as Giancarlo Stanton insurance), and Anthony Volpe’s re-ascension. — Marco F.
What the Yankees decide to do at second base is one of the most fascinating storylines of the offseason.
Advertisement
I agree with you, Marco, that this season has likely cost Chisholm millions. He is nearing the end of his worst offensive season since 2021. He won’t reach the heights he set for himself entering 2026, but he still could reach a 20-40 season. Few players have the talent to post those numbers. Before this year, Chisholm posted back-to-back 4+ fWAR seasons. It would not be wrong for the Yankees or another team to bet on his upside.
Chisholm still offers tremendous defense at second and excellent baserunning. If his bat gets back to being considerably above average, he profiles as one of the best second basemen in the sport. There are valid concerns about his offense, though. His hit tool is considerably below average, and as he ages and loses athleticism, that could be a major problem that he cannot overcome.
The Yankees should consider giving Chisholm a short-term deal, though. He is a better option than Caballero and Volpe, who are better as role players, and few available players are better than what he can provide.
The Yankees should strongly consider playing Caballero or Volpe, who played a few games in the minors there, at third base. McMahon is one of the worst everyday regulars in the big leagues this season, and there’s a higher likelihood of Caballero or Volpe producing at the plate.
Has the Martian played his last game in a Yankees uniform? — oconnell13
It’s a hard question to answer because you can’t predict injuries. You never know if the Yankees will have to reach into the minor leagues for depth.
But it’s not far-fetched to think Jasson Domínguez will never play in another important game for the Yankees again. He cannot be trusted in the field. Every game matters for the Yankees, and there’s always a queasy feeling when the ball is hit his way.
His bat also hasn’t progressed enough to keep giving him chances to prove himself. Jones has leapfrogged him on the depth chart, and the Yankees now have Heliot Ramos on their roster. There may not be space for Domínguez.

What are the Yankees’ pitching plans for the rest of the regular season? Specifically, who’s lining up for the Rays series and will any of them be limited in terms of pitch count? — Nick B.
As of now, the Yankees are lined up to start their best four starters against the Rays next week. Here’s how it looks:
Tuesday: Fried and Rodón are in line to start the games of the doubleheader.
Wednesday: Cole
Thursday: Schlittler
The Rays are also on track to start their best pitchers for that series. They could start Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen on Tuesday, Freddy Peralta on Wednesday and Ian Seymour on Thursday. Their rotation is dependent on what they decide to do for their weekend series against the Boston Red Sox. But if they wanted, all of these pitchers could factor into their pitching plans next week.
Any chance the Yanks consider Ben Rice as the backup catcher on the postseason roster to free up an extra bench spot for someone more versatile (and better than) Ali Sánchez/J.C. Escarra? — Matthew L.
The odds of this happening are close to zero.
Earlier in the season, Rice kept catching behind the scenes. Before games, he’d catch bullpens and do on-field drills with director of catching Tanner Swanson. Rice hasn’t done any of that in months.
If anything, Rice would only be used in an emergency situation. Believe it or not, the organization believes in Sánchez. That’s why they didn’t promote Mitch Garver. Sánchez is out of minor league options, so they’d have to designate him for assignment and risk him getting claimed off waivers. They value the consistency he provides to their pitchers, and they think he’s a better defender than the metrics show.

Yankees RHP Clarke Schmidt Returns As Reliever After 14-Month Rehab
The New York Yankees returned right-handed pitcher Clarke Schmidt from his rehabilitation assignment and reinstated him from the injured list on Wednesday, aiming to integrate the 30-year-old into their bullpen for the postseason following his 14-month recovery from elbow surgery.
Schmidt had an internal brace procedure on his ulnar collateral ligament on July 11, 2025, and began minor league rehab on Aug. 29. The 2017 first-round draft pick was used exclusively as a starter since 2023, but with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Carlos Rodon and Gerrit Cole in the rotation, Schmidt will transition to relief.
"It's been a long journey, a lot of work that goes into this. A lot of long days, early mornings," Schmidt said before the game Wednesday against the Minnesota Twins. "I've just been itching to come back."
The Yankees designated popular multi-position player Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment to make room on the 40-man roster for Schmidt. Cabrera missed most of the 2025 season with a severe ankle injury.
"I’m blessed to have a lot of guys on this team that you just admire and respect and love doing the job with on a daily basis," manager Aaron Boone said. "Oswaldo’s right there at the top of that list."
Reporting by The Associated Press.

The Yankees reinstated Clarke Schmidt from the 60-day injured list ahead of today’s series finale in Minnesota. The team also optioned right-handed reliever Bradley Hanner to Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, and designated Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment.
It’s the end of a long road back for Schmidt, who hasn’t pitched on a major league mound since July 2025 after undergoing Tommy John surgery. At the time, Schmidt was in the midst of establishing himself as one of the Yankees’ best starters, running a 3.07 ERA across 164 innings between 2024 and 2025.
Schmidt won’t have enough time to build up to a starter’s workload prior to the postseason, but he has a real chance to make an impact in the Yankee bullpen. He’s been used in one-to-two inning stretches in the minors, where his fastball has sat around his customary 94 mph. Beyond David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, and Brent Headrick, the Yankees have little set in stone in their bullpen, leaving a wide opportunity for someone like Schmidt to grab a meaningful role with a strong showing in the final two weeks of the season.
The Yankees had to manage their 40-man roster as a result of this move, and Cabrera was sadly the casualty. Schmidt coming off the 60-day IL necessitated clearing a spot on a full 40-man. Cabrera, who has spent most of the season at Triple-A after recovering from a gruesome knee injury last year, drew the short stick. The Yankees could have plausibly transferred Fernando Cruz to the 60-day IL, but instead opted to keep hope alive for a return from Cruz.

The Yankees’ pitching picture continues to regain its health, as Clarke Schmidt was reinstated from the 60-day injured list on Wednesday as he returns from Tommy John surgery.
The 30-year-old right-hander had been out since July 3 of last season when he was diagnosed with a torn UCL that not only required Tommy John surgery, but also an internal brace procedure. He had a 3.32 ERA and a 1.090 WHIP in 14 starts last season before the injury
He should be in play for a full-time spot in the rotation next season. Over 30 starts between the 2024 and 2025 seasons, he sported a 3.07 ERA and a 1.140 WHIP, which would make an already-great starting five that much more elite.
In the immediate future, though, Schmidt will likely spend this upcoming postseason in the bullpen. Shortened rotations would likely see the Yankees roll with four starters, and there is no usurping Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, or Carlos Rodon.
To make room for him on the 40-man roster, the Yankees designated utilityman Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment. He played just three games with the big-league club this season, spending most of his time with Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre. The 27-year-old was slashing .288/.345/.444 in 122 games, but owned a .635 career OPS across parts of five seasons with the Yankees.

MINNEAPOLIS — When the Yankees wrapped up their spot in the postseason Monday night, Aaron Boone joined some select company.
He became the second manager in MLB history to reach the postseason in at least eight of his first nine seasons, joining Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, who has now done it in each of his first 11 seasons. Boone is also the third manager to make the playoffs in eight of his first nine seasons with the Yankees, joining Joe Torre and Casey Stengel.

Of course, Roberts, Torre and Stengel have combined to win 14 World Series titles while Boone is still in search of his first. And ultimately, in New York, that is how he will be judged, as opposed to just getting his team to the postseason regularly.
But in a season in which the Yankees have had most of their biggest stars spend sizable chunks of time on the injured list, Boone has helped lead them through the adversity to still have as good a chance as any team in the American League to make a run to the World Series.
“He’s our guy,” Aaron Judge said in the champagne-soaked visitors clubhouse at Target Field late Monday night. “He’s the one we go to battle for every single night and just lucky and blessed to have him here, to be able to fight for a guy like that. He loves every single guy in this room and we’re going to fight till the end for him.”
The Yankees still have bigger things left to accomplish this year, starting with trying to chase down the Rays for the division, but then more importantly, attempting to go the distance in October for the first time since 2009.
But by the time they clinched their playoff spot, the Yankees had survived 84 games without Judge; 124 games and counting without Giancarlo Stanton; 25 games without Cody Bellinger; 27 games and counting without Trent Grisham (across two IL stints); 22 games without Ryan McMahon (across two IL stints); 51 games without Gerrit Cole; 71 games without Max Fried (across two IL stints); 40 games without Carlos Rodón (across two IL stints); 21 games and counting without Ryan Weathers; and 150 games and counting without Clarke Schmidt, among others.
Every team deals with injuries, but not every team survives them to the extent that the Yankees have, entering Tuesday on pace to match the 94 wins they have had in each of the last two seasons.
“It’s very tough for a Yankee manager to win Manager of the Year,” bench coach Brad Ausmus said Tuesday, pointing to the high expectations with which the franchise enters every season. “Obviously [Rays manager] Kevin Cash and [White Sox manager] Will Venable will be extremely strong candidates. But with the job [Boone] has done this year with the injuries, keeping the group as one cohesive unit, I think he should definitely be in the discussion.”
There were some rough stretches along the way during Judge’s three-month absence, most notably a 5-15 skid from late June to early July.
Shop Yankees Merch
Even when the Yankees started to snap out of that, it did not often feel like it as their offense was still in a malaise and almost every game they played was a low-scoring, nail-biting battle.
Though that stretch threatens to ultimately cost the Yankees a chance at overtaking the Rays for the AL East, Boone is hoping he will have his team in a position to be at its best in the postseason to make a run at an elusive title.
“It’s not easy,” Austin Wells said. “You lose guys left and right at different parts of the season. Having to piece wins together, keep us right there in the division race throughout the whole year, he does an impressive job. Definitely a testament to him. Looking forward to more of that, more winning decisions and keep leading us.”

Another season, another spot secured in the postseason for the New York Yankees. Mirroring last year’s path, the Yanks are once again hunting for a World Series berth. With Jazz Chisholm Jr.’s return date drawing near, New York is aiming to finally snap its long championship drought.
However, when speaking with Randy Miller of NJ.com, Chisholm revealed that his long-term future in the Bronx remains uncertain, noting he hasn’t discussed a contract extension since spring training. “It was just like, ‘We don’t do extensions,'” Chisholm admitted.
While trade rumors have occasionally linked Chisholm to the crosstown rival New York Mets, his latest candid comments suggest he could very well be playing elsewhere next season.
Meanwhile, the Yankees confirmed a target return date for starter Clarke Schmidt as the postseason approaches. Manager Aaron Boone expects to have the right-hander fully stretched out and ready to bolster the rotation for October.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. #13 of the New York Yankees.
Chisholm Jr. ‘reaches out’ to the Yankees front office
When asked if he had formally approached the front office or General Manager Brian Cashman about an extension, Chisholm clarified that it wasn’t a sit-down meeting, but rather a brief exchange in passing.
“I wouldn’t say I reached out. It was more of a mutual thing, just me walking around saying something to Cashman as he walked past me,” Chisholm said, as reported by Miller.
How well did Chisholm Jr. play this season?
Chisholm has delivered his signature blend of dynamic speed and raw power during his 2026 campaign with the Yankees, even if his overall production has suffered from brief stretches of inconsistency. Here is a look at his statistical output this year:

New York Daily News | Peter Sblendorio: After taking two of three from the Mets, the Yankees control their own playoff destiny to a point. Their magic number is down to one, a win over the Twins on Monday or a Blue Jays loss to Detroit would send New York back to the postseason. While a division title is improbable, but not impossible, the first Wild Card slot seems all but ensured, giving the club home field in a best-of-three series.

Sanchez: The Yankee bullpen has ranked amongst the best in baseball, but the eighth and ninth guys in your relief corps are always going to be borderline — see Hanner, Bradley. Clarke Schmidt, an established MLBer, has completed his rehab assignment returning from Tommy John surgery, and is set to be activated during this week's series in Minnesota. Schmidt is likely a much better option to fill in one of those bullpen slots, boosting the floor of a squad that boasts a pretty high ceiling.

Hopefully this will be enough to quell this outbreak, and nobody else will be at risk of being sick.
